column2: Act Six
Beware of Fire, Thieves, and Your Senior
Beware of Your Senior

What a wonderful morning. Sunlight poured through the skylight onto Xia Mi. The slender, supple girl stood on one leg with the grace of a ballerina, reaching out to steal two cups of Coke for them. Lu Mingfei watched her long leg lifted into the sunlight, every line youthful and fluid, every inch of skin smooth as jade. For the first time he understood what the ancients meant by a perfect balance of flesh and bone.
“TRY A WEEK WITHOUT RAILWAY!!!” proclaimed a huge white banner hanging in the empty waiting hall of Chicago's train station.
Lu Mingfei lifted his face to the ceiling and sighed, his heart sinking.

They had flown halfway around the world to Chicago and hurried eagerly to the station, only to find a waiting hall littered with scraps of paper, placards, and drink cans. A few hours before they landed at Chicago International Airport, the entire Chicago railway workforce had finished marching in protest and gone home. They would not be back for a week.
They were on strike.

Lu Mingfei had grown up under the red flag of socialism and had always been generous with his praise of strikes. When his high-school politics teacher put a question about the strike movement on the final exam, he had even quoted Comrade Lenin with feeling: “How profound is the influence of a strike! Every strike powerfully turns the workers' thoughts toward socialism, toward the struggle the whole working class must wage to free itself from the oppression of capital!”

But supporting the Chicago railway workers out of his own wallet hurt. Cassell operated the CC1000 branch express itself, but without switch operators or a dispatch center, every train had to stop. They would certainly miss registration. Since the delay was beyond their control, their GPA would not be penalized, but the college would not pay for a week in Chicago.
“Then we'll stay in Chicago for a week,” Chu Zihang said calmly. “If that's a problem for you, share a room with me. I'll pay.”
A sneaky little thrill ran through Lu Mingfei. He had known his expressionless senior never quibbled over money. He had been waiting for exactly those words!
He hoisted his luggage. “Come on! Let's go get a room!”
A soft giggle came from overhead. “What do two grown men need a room for?”

Lu Mingfei jumped. He and Chu Zihang were clearly the only people in the hall. Could Lu Mingze have grown restless again? He looked up for the voice and saw the enormous white banner, ten meters wide and ten meters long, trembling slightly, as if someone were hiding behind it. A human shape moved left along the beam. A hand emerged from behind the cloth and unfastened the hook on the left. Then the figure moved right, and the hand reached out again for the other hook.
“Careful!” Chu Zihang said suddenly.

He saw the beam wobble. The person behind the banner lost their balance and pulled the whole sheet down. Just then a gust swept through the waiting hall, and the white cloth fell like a cloud. Chu Zihang and Lu Mingfei both lunged to catch the person: a fall from five or six meters up would break an ordinary person's bones. Lu Mingfei had barely taken two steps when the cloth came down over his head. He panicked, tripped, and fell flat on his face like a fallen angel. Chu Zihang was half a step slower, but he could see the figure wrapped in the cloth, and caught them securely.
The person was startlingly light.
“Who? Who are you? Are you trying to get yourself killed? You made me fall too!” Lu Mingfei scrambled up, rubbing his back and complaining without pause.
A head poked out of the white cloth and looked around. For a moment both Lu Mingfei and Chu Zihang fell silent. Chu Zihang gently set the person down and stepped back.

It was respect for a woman, and awe before beauty. A tomb robber crawling into Tutankhamun's burial chamber, confronted by that exquisite golden mask as if time itself had been sealed inside it, might likewise fall silent in wonder and hesitate to lift it, afraid of disturbing sleeping beauty, afraid she would grow old the moment she woke.
The girl regarded them curiously. In her clear eyes, both boys saw their own awkward, self-conscious reflections.

As a shut-in, Lu Mingfei kept a mental ranking of beautiful girls. Nono and Su Xiaoqiang tied for first. The little witch needed no explanation, and Su Xiaoqiang's nickname, the Little Celestial Princess, was well earned. Her mother was Portuguese, giving her the defined features of a European and the gentle beauty of an Eastern girl. Zero ranked second: Her Ice Queen Majesty's beauty hovered between girl and little girl, proud as snow and ice, though she was always so cold-faced that she seemed to think the whole world owed her millions of rubles. Liu Miaomiao came third, while Chen Wenwen was only fourth, even allowing for the likelihood that judge Lu Mingfei had awarded her extra points for personal preference.
Yet none of them could quite be called flawless. “Flawless” was not really a good word; every living thing had defects. A truly flawless face probably existed only beneath a sculptor's chisel.
But looking at this girl, you felt as though the sculpture had opened its eyes and come to life.
“Hi there, monster!” Lu Mingfei murmured.
He meant that only a monster could be that beautiful. His expressionless senior and the beauty herself could hardly be expected to understand a joke with such depth.
Chu Zihang nudged him with an elbow. “She's a fellow student.”
The girl bared her teeth. “Not a monster. I'm a sweet, gentle girl!”
Lu Mingfei was delighted. Someone did understand his joke after all. Only then did he notice the black ticket held between her teeth: a special ticket for the CC1000 branch express.
“Chu Zihang, mechanical engineering.” Chu Zihang reached out to help her up.

The girl emerged from the white cloth. She wore a plain white spaghetti-strap top with batik orchids, very short shorts, ankle socks, and sneakers. Her outfit was simple, with sunglasses perched on her head.
“Senior!” The girl sprang up. “I'm a freshman, Xia Mi.”
“Hey, hey, don't block me.” Lu Mingfei shouldered Chu Zihang aside. “I'm a senior too! Lu Mingfei, history.”
“Oh, a humanities guy?” Xia Mi widened her eyes and looked him up and down.

For no reason Lu Mingfei felt inferior to Chu Zihang. Strictly speaking, Chu Zihang's department was called Alchemical Mechanical Engineering and specialized in alchemical equipment. Lu Mingfei's history department was really Dragon Genealogy, where he would study dragon family trees and dig deep into the dark side of their history. But none of that was easy to explain to this junior, still as blank as a sheet of paper. The mystery would be revealed at freshman orientation.
“What were you doing up there?” Chu Zihang asked.

“Taking down this sheet. We'd have to stay in a hotel for a week, and I'm out of money. I still have to save up for a lens for my camera. Nobody needs this thing anyway, so I can use it to pitch a tent near Central Park and sleep there for a week.” Xia Mi plopped down amid the cloth and folded the huge sheet. Her hands moved quickly. Soon she had rolled it into an enormous bundle and slung it over her shoulder. “I'll be going, then. See you at college!”
“Can you pitch a tent in the park?” Chu Zihang asked.

“I'll tell them I'm demonstrating on behalf of the Chicago railway workers!” Xia Mi clenched her fist, earnest and blazing with civic spirit. “If our railway brothers aren't going back to work, I'll share their hardship!”
“Brilliant! I can go with you!” Lu Mingfei was delighted by her ingenuity.
Chu Zihang hesitated. “You don't have a Social Security card yet. It could be awkward if the police questioned you. If you don't mind, you could stay with us. We're going to...”
“Get a room?” Xia Mi spun around and stared at him.

Chu Zihang froze, taken aback by the fierce look in her eyes. He realized the invitation was inappropriate. They might be fellow students, but they hardly knew one another. Two boys inviting a girl to share a room, a Chinese girl at that—her parents would probably throw gas cylinders at them if they found out.
“A rich guy! I'm so happy! Please keep me!” The next moment Xia Mi was pretending to collapse against Chu Zihang's chest.
Chu Zihang stood there silently, wondering whether he had met a female Fingel or a female Lu Mingfei. Well, there was not much difference between the two species.

“Come on, come on, let's get a room! I'm starving.” Lu Mingfei picked up Xia Mi's luggage. Compared with other students arriving in America, she had brought very little: one standard suitcase and a tote bag.
“Wait, wait, let me get another Coke,” Xia Mi said.
“Buy one after we get to the hotel,” Chu Zihang said.
“All you ever say is buy, buy, buy!” Xia Mi made a face. “I never said I was going to pay.”

She fished a used paper Coke cup out of her bag and trotted to the entrance of a closed Subway. Standing on tiptoe, she squeezed half her body between the metal bars. With the cup in her hand she could just reach the soda dispenser. A wonderfully refreshing sound of flowing liquid followed: the Subway staff had forgotten to unplug the machine when they closed.
Xia Mi sipped her Coke, looking pleased with herself. “I didn't arrive two hours before you for nothing. I've already scouted the whole place!”
“Wow! Doesn't that mean endless free Coke?” Lu Mingfei was overjoyed. “I'll get one too.”
“You boys won't fit through. I'll get some for you.” Xia Mi produced two more paper cups.

What a wonderful morning. Sunlight poured through the skylight onto Xia Mi. The slender, supple girl stood on one leg with the grace of a ballerina, reaching out to steal two cups of Coke for them. Lu Mingfei watched her long leg lifted into the sunlight, every line youthful and fluid, every inch of skin smooth as jade. For the first time he understood what the ancients meant by a perfect balance of flesh and bone. Watching her was simply an appreciation of beauty; he felt neither lust nor unbearable longing. He only wished the cups were bigger so she would take longer to fill them, and at the same time wanted to pull out his phone and preserve the moment.
It was as wonderful as the first time the guys had sneaked into a dance academy and watched the pretty girls practice through the glass, a sight to lift the heart.
Pretty little female thieves were truly one of the cutest species in the world!
“Drink the Coke I stole and you'll owe me a favor. You'll have to help me out later,” Xia Mi said as the three of them dragged their luggage toward the exit.
“Of course! Your senior's got your back!” Lu Mingfei drank his Coke and thumped his chest.

Only a fool would fail to look after a junior like this. Here was that legendary, wondrous species, the junior girl! She was electricity, she was light, she was an awesome myth! She had come to rescue suffering seniors from their sea of misery! In every story about junior girls, they admired the knowledgeable, cultured seniors who knew all the rules for surviving campus life. Wasn't this how generations of seniors studying in America had got by? Drive a battered car to the airport to meet a junior, enthusiastically help her find a place to live, generously drive her to the supermarket, take her to an amusement park to expose the decadence of capitalism, and confess your love before she had fully learned her way around America and discovered you were just a loser! Generation after generation, the seniors had taken the juniors' share, leaving the younger boys to wait silently until they became seniors themselves and a new crop of junior girls descended from heaven.
Junior girls were like chives: every crop was fresher than the last!

“You're so kind, senior.” Xia Mi smiled a smile that could win anyone's heart and make flowers bloom. Then her voice suddenly dropped, like an older sister offering a confidence. “Xia Mi, be careful he doesn't pick you up. Stay alert! Beware of fire, thieves, and your senior!”
In a guest room at the Hyatt Regency Chicago, Lu Mingfei lounged on the sofa watching television.

The famous hotel stood beside the Chicago River. Outside, white tour boats glided slowly past, a plump Black guide at the bow enthusiastically recounting the golden years of the city's founding to a group of foreign tourists.

“Senior, isn't this a little inappropriate? I absolutely support you paying for our junior's room,” Lu Mingfei said, “but two guys and a girl in one room? Won't the Disciplinary Committee come after us?”

“The Disciplinary Committee doesn't care about that. Professor Manstein is probably arranging defenses for this year's Freedom Day,” Chu Zihang said mildly. “I don't think it's quite appropriate either, but she said if I paid for a separate room, she'd owe me too much, and she'd rather pitch a tent in the park.”

He stood with his back against the wall, leafing through an old annotated edition of the Emerald Tablet, a reference work for Alchemical Chemistry III. The Emerald Tablet was an ancient text from 1900 BC, engraved on an emerald slab and discovered in a hidden chamber beneath a pyramid. Considered the foundational book of alchemy, it claimed as its author Hermes, the three-in-one god of Egyptian mythology. It contained only thirteen sentences, yet held all the truths of alchemy.
Water splashed in the next room. Xia Mi was bathing in the bathroom.

“It rises from earth to heaven and descends again from heaven to earth, receiving the power of the higher and the lower. Thus you shall gain the glory of the world and be free of darkness and ignorance,” Chu Zihang murmured. This was Newton's translation of the Emerald Tablet. The scientist himself was also a well-known mystic, deeply interested in alchemy and the occult. In the Middle Ages theology and science were not so clearly separated, and alchemy counted as a science too.

Lu Mingfei was truly in awe of him. They had finally found a girl among the freshmen beautiful enough to be the campus belle, and they were even sharing a room. They ought to drink a few beers and get to know one another. Imagine it: their pretty junior bathing next door. Ah, “warm spring waters caressed her creamy skin.” Back in class, the more the teacher explained the Song of Everlasting Sorrow, the more irritated he had become. Now, wiping away his drool as he imagined water dancing over his junior's lovely skin, he felt enlightened at last and understood classmate Bai Letian's poetic vision. Come to think of it, wasn't that line downright indecent? Recite it to yourself a few times and you could feel a nosebleed coming on... Yet Chu Zihang looked utterly unmoved, having wrestled with that dry reference book for nearly half an hour. Such meditative powers would be wasted on anyone but a monk.
“Senior, I know you're studying, but couldn't you find somewhere to sit?” Lu Mingfei could not understand why Chu Zihang kept standing against the wall.
“I'm practicing my standing posture at the same time. I stand for half an hour every night. It's very good for the spine. I suggest you try it,” Chu Zihang said.

Lu Mingfei glanced at him. “Forget it. Fingel would die laughing if he saw.” Such dull, strenuous self-discipline, with its faint air of aristocratic refinement, struck him as a little silly, though it suited Chu Zihang rather well.

“Newton's original says, ‘It ascends from ye earth to ye heaven & again it descends to ye earth and receives ye force of things superior & inferior. By this means you shall have ye glory of ye whole world & thereby all obscurity shall fly from you.’ It can also be translated, ‘The One rises from earth to heaven, then descends again to earth, absorbing the powers of the upper and lower realms. Thus you shall possess the glory of the whole world and be free of ignorance.’” The bathroom door opened. Wrapped in a bathrobe, Xia Mi emerged, drying her long hair, and went to the wall opposite Chu Zihang. She too stood with her back against it. “The key to understanding the passage is what that ‘it’ refers to.”
“It could mean the material used in alchemy: metal or another substance being scorched by flame,” Chu Zihang said.
“It could also mean the spirit,” Xia Mi said.
“There hasn't been much progress on the spirit interpretation since 1972.”
“But a new paper on it came out just last year.”

The two people standing against the walls exchanged questions and answers with easy fluency, while Lu Mingfei stared wide-eyed. He was like a toad listening to a sermon before the Buddha: he could hear profound truths but understood not a word, and wished someone would translate the mysteries into ribbits.
“Wait, wait, what are you talking about? Junior, why are you standing against the wall too?” Lu Mingfei could not take it anymore.

“The Emerald Tablet. Senior Lu, didn't you take Alchemical Chemistry? It's a surviving fragment of a draconic classic. It's just so obscure that no one's ever given it a definitive interpretation,” Xia Mi said. “I'm waiting for my hair to dry and practicing my posture at the same time.”
“What did you say?” Lu Mingfei was stunned.

What was going on? This junior had not even been through orientation. Wasn't she supposed to be a blank sheet on which the most beautiful picture could be painted? On hearing that a miraculous reptilian dynasty really existed in the world, she ought to scream in terror! Back then, Senior Lu Mingfei himself had screamed and practically wet his pants!
“Dragons, dragons, dragons,” Xia Mi said three times.

“She was in the preparatory program. Prep students take the 3E exam early, so the existence of dragons isn't a secret to her. Her bloodline is A-rank, exceptionally good,” Chu Zihang explained to Lu Mingfei.
“Preparatory? What program?”

“The college's secret branch in China. It selects high-school students with bloodlines from across the country for preparatory classes. The college gives them the 3E exam early. If their bloodlines are good enough, they go straight to the main campus after graduation. If they don't pass, the Gate to Cassell begins its closing sequence. They're treated as ordinary students and take the national college entrance exam when they graduate.” Chu Zihang continued, “Xia Mi, born October 30, 1993, in Beijing, China. Female. Before the preparatory program she attended the high school affiliated with Peking University. Registered in Beijing. Family consists of her parents and an older brother.”
“Hey!” Xia Mi glared. “Are you checking my household registration?”
“Norma sent the information from the main campus. We need to know who you are.” Chu Zihang picked up his iPad from a little table. “Lu Mingfei, hand this to Xia Mi for me.”
“Why am I the errand boy?” Lu Mingfei muttered.
“I haven't finished my exercise.” Chu Zihang was still standing perfectly straight, now balancing a hardcover book on his head.
Four or five meters away, Xia Mi also balanced a hardcover on her head and held out her hand, waiting for Lu Mingfei to bring her the iPad.
“Are you two kidding me?” Lu Mingfei snatched the iPad from Chu Zihang and ran it over to Xia Mi, looking every inch an obedient little lackey.

The iPad held Xia Mi's file, thorough and clear down to the smallest detail. Cassell College's Intelligence Department was responsible for student records. Famous for CIA-like rigor, its people made everyone's file read like a catalog of embarrassing secrets. Xia Mi's photograph brightened the document, a casual close-up taken with some small camera. Her hair was dyed dark coffee brown, she wore dark cosmetic contact lenses, and she was looking back against a sunset, a yellow bow in her hair flying in the breeze.
“You're so alternative!” Lu Mingfei commented offhandedly.
“You're the pig, and your whole family's a bunch of pigs.” Xia Mi took the iPad and glanced at it. “I was cosplaying Haruhi Suzumiya at the anime club.”
“They picked you to cosplay Haruhi Suzumiya?”
“I wanted to cosplay Asahina originally,” Xia Mi said.
“Asahina?” Lu Mingfei grinned, delighted.

Asahina was the big-busted beauty in The Melancholy of Haruhi Suzumiya, always forced to dress as a bunny girl, a maid, or even a sexy frog. Imagining Xia Mi in the role, he felt another nosebleed threatening.
Xia Mi sighed and looked down at her chest. After a moment's silence, she said, “But they all disagreed. They said I didn't qualify...”
“I hate girls with big breasts the most!” Xia Mi suddenly looked up and shouted. “They bully people!”
The words came straight from the heart and rang with conviction. The room went quiet. No... it fell deathly silent.
“Well... my condolences.” Lu Mingfei handed his discouraged junior an orange and patted the book on her head, like a compassionate monk comforting a young seeker short on natural gifts.

Then he burst out laughing, threw himself onto the bed, buried his head under the covers, and pounded the mattress. He could not hold it in any longer; bottling it up would have caused internal injuries. Suddenly the strike seemed wonderful, and the coming week stranded in Chicago would be even better, all because he had met this pretty, mischievous, delightfully goofy junior. She was both Lin Zhiling and a stand-up comedian!
“Laugh... laugh at your own sister.” Xia Mi glanced at Lu Mingfei and curled her lip.
“If ‘the One’ means the spirit, then do the upper and lower realms refer to the different spiritual worlds of dragons and humans?”
“You can interpret it that way. It describes the process of a human evolving into a dragon and thereby reaching self-completion.”
“Can humans evolve into dragons?”

“Some medieval scholars of the Emerald Tablet believed it was a work falsely attributed to a god, but that its author had ‘approached infinitely close to godhood’ and ‘stolen the laws of the gods.’ Fearing ordinary people would discover those laws, the author used secret language.”
“The hieratic script of ancient Egypt?”

“Yes. Only priests knew hieratic script. Arabic replaced Egyptian as the common language of Egypt in the seventh century, so hieratic is hard to decipher. The Newton translation you're using could be full of errors...”

“The translation you just used says, ‘The One rises from earth to heaven, then descends again to earth, absorbing the powers of the upper and lower realms. Thus you shall possess the glory of the whole world and be free of ignorance.’ By your interpretation, if a human can evolve into a dragon, there would be no need to return to the human world. Since the author wanted to leave ignorance behind...” Chu Zihang pondered.
“Why leave cute girls behind?” Lu Mingfei interrupted, bored out of his mind.

It was a beautiful day: a luxurious five-star hotel, a comfortable big sofa, a complimentary fruit platter, a rich expressionless senior paying the bill, and a pretty junior he had just met. Yet the two of them stood against the walls to either side of Lu Mingfei, each balancing a book on their head like a pair of door gods. Worse still, after reading separately for a while, the two door gods had started arguing over how to interpret that Emerald Tablet. Both were damn academics, and Lu Mingfei did not understand a word, hearing only mystical phrases like “from heaven to earth” and “from earth to heaven.”

“Then why must he ‘descend again to earth’? Isn't ‘from earth to heaven’ the ultimate goal of all alchemy?” Chu Zihang had no intention of paying Lu Mingfei any attention; his mind was entirely occupied with the subject he was discussing with Xia Mi.

“From earth to heaven, from heaven to earth, how marvelous are all the things in the world, how marvelous...” Lu Mingfei suddenly remembered a children's song from a CCTV program he had watched as a child and sang it offhandedly.
Chu Zihang and Xia Mi stared at him speechlessly, apparently unable to understand his inner world at all.

“Between heaven and earth there hangs a scale, and the common people are its weight...” Just as Lu Mingfei realized he had gone off the rails again, Xia Mi suddenly began singing the theme from Prime Minister Liu Luoguo in the style of Beijing drum singing.
“Hey, what's going on? Weren't you having an academic discussion? How did we suddenly turn it into a medley of old songs?” Lu Mingfei said.
“I was playing along with you,” Xia Mi said. “Do you know the theme from Barbapapa?”
“I think I remember it...” Chu Zihang tried humming the tune.

Later, remembering that warm, sunlit afternoon, Lu Mingfei felt that they had done nothing meaningful at all. Tour boats came and went on the Chicago River, The Simpsons played in reruns on television, and he sat on the sofa with a handsome boy and a beautiful girl standing straight on either side, hardcovers balanced on their heads. Sometimes they discussed scholarship, sometimes they sang back and forth. Sometimes Xia Mi told silly jokes, and sometimes Lu Mingfei explained the college's factions to her. An afternoon like that sounded like a waste of life.
And yet you always wished such afternoons could be longer, more frequent, and never end...
“Are you asleep?” Lu Mingfei asked softly, looking at the ceiling.
The person beside him was also looking at the ceiling, the blanket pulled up to the shoulders, both hands neatly tucked beneath it. “Not yet. I'm thinking.”
“Sorry, sorry. Was I too loud turning over?”
“No. I'm just not used to sleeping with someone else. I'll fall asleep when I get tired. It's all right.”
“You have an iPhone too, and there's Wi-Fi here. Since neither of us can sleep... how about a game of tile matching online?” Lu Mingfei suggested after a long silence.
“I don't know how to play tile matching, but we could play chess.”
“You've never even played tile matching? Senior, your life is a tragedy...” Lu Mingfei turned his head and sighed at the handsome face and neat eyelashes beside him.
“Sorry,” Chu Zihang said.

Lu Mingfei remembered the time during high-school military training when the boys had eavesdropped on the girls' late-night conversation. The subject had been: “What would I do if I landed Chu Zihang?” The aggressive faction insisted they would push him down. The literary faction wanted to hear him tell bedtime stories. The devoted-wife-and-mother faction wanted to feed their darling Chu Zihang baby until he was plump and healthy. The career-minded faction scoffed: “I'd let him follow me and live the life he wants! I'll support him!” In the end the sentimental faction won out when a girl said softly, “I just want to count his eyelashes one by one while he sleeps...” The boys listening at the wall all went weak at the knees.
Time had passed and things had changed. The girls from that conversation probably all had boyfriends now, while one of the eavesdroppers was sharing a bed and pillow with young master Chu.
“Damn it,” Lu Mingfei muttered inwardly. “A whole week in bed with this young master? What have I done to deserve it? Hey, girls, jealous of me? Hey, girls, jealous?”
He muttered himself to sleep.

Chu Zihang turned his head. Xia Mi was already fast asleep. The curtains were open, and moonlight fell across her soft bangs. The blanket was wrapped all the way up to the back of her head, leaving only her small, delicate face exposed. Her long eyelashes cast two shadows on her cheeks. Something stirred in Chu Zihang's heart. Each lash could be counted distinctly, as though marking the passage of time.

At the college's main campus, in the central control room, an aluminum security case sat on the long table with a courier label from China attached. The last CC1000 express before the strike had brought it there.

Schneider shone a dark-purple flashlight along the edge of the case. Under the ultraviolet light a reflective security label appeared, like the marks used to authenticate banknotes. He nodded. “The seal is intact. The case wasn't opened on the way. What's inside is safe.”
“This didn't need to come to the college. It could have gone straight to the Board of Trustees,” Manstein said, frowning. “Now we have to wait for them to send someone to collect it.”

“I told Chu Zihang to send it to us,” Schneider said. “I'm still not entirely reassured. We'd better open it and have a look.” He acted as soon as he spoke, picking up handheld hydraulic cutters and snipping off the lock with a snap.
“Hey!” Manstein shouted, trying to stop him, but it was too late.

“You work like a burglar breaking down a door. Don't you have a key?” Manstein said. “Leave it alone. It isn't what we're after. We've recovered it as the Board of Trustees ordered, so let them have it. Don't touch it. You'll only make trouble for yourself.”
“It's simpler this way,” Schneider said mildly. Sometimes Manstein had to wonder whether Chu Zihang had learned certain habits from his violence-prone teacher.

Inside the aluminum case was a sealed paper envelope with its seal intact. Schneider tore it open and emptied it onto the table. The envelope contained photocopied documents printed on transparent film. Schneider flipped through them at astonishing speed. His hands suddenly became extraordinarily nimble, nothing like an old man's. The sheets slid rapidly between his fingers as his eyes swept over them like a scanner, his iron-gray pupils contracted to pinpoints. Manstein had rarely seen him so intent.
“Hey, you! Are you crazy?” Manstein finally understood and shouted.
Schneider was not checking whether the material was intact at all. He meant to scan it before it was taken away, stealing a look at the Board of Trustees' top-secret SS-rank files.

“Do you know what this is?” Schneider's face was expressionless, and he showed no sign of stopping. “These are confidential Chinese police files from the past five years on ‘unknown types of crime.’ That means supernatural crime. This archive is like the US Air Force's Project Blue Book on UFOs. Of course, most cases simply involved methods too ingenious to solve, but some are connected to dragons.”
“The Chinese police know dragons exist?” Guderian was shocked.

“No, but they know these events are beyond ordinary human understanding. Take this one.” Schneider laid a sheet of film on the table. “On July 3, 2004, Typhoon Dandelion made landfall on China's southeastern coast, bringing three days of storms. During that storm there was an incident that was never explained. A Maybach sedan was abandoned on an elevated road, its body covered with inexplicable damage, as if it had been repeatedly stamped by machinery and then cut with a laser welding torch. The driver was not in the car. No one ever saw him again; he vanished from the world.” Schneider spoke slowly. “That driver was Chu Zihang's biological father.”
“No wonder the Board of Trustees didn't make Chu Zihang the commissioner...” Manstein understood at last. They had had no choice but to use Chu Zihang, yet they could not trust him.

Manstein turned and backed away step by step from the long table. “Schneider, I can't stop you from protecting your student, but I have nothing to do with this! You'll be punished under college regulations... no, under the Party's rules!”

He chaired the Disciplinary Committee and oversaw college discipline, but above college rules stood the rules of the Secret Party. Those rules derived from an ancient alchemical scroll, the Abraham Bloodline Covenant, a harsh code handed down from the Middle Ages. Schneider had violated the Council of Elders' secrets, an offense approaching treason in its gravity.
“No, this concerns you.” Without looking up, Schneider handed Manstein an envelope he had prepared in advance. “See for yourself.”
Manstein opened the envelope. Inside were student dossiers, each bearing a special red wax seal. The words on the seals read: “Nibelungen Project.”
“Nibelungen?” Manstein had heard of this mythical “realm of the dead,” but he did not see what it had to do with him.
Then his face changed. Turning through several dossiers, he saw the name Chen Motong.
“Why are you flipping through so fast? I saw Lu Mingfei...” Guderian craned his neck to look too.
“What does this mean?” Manstein asked quietly.

“The Nibelungen Project is a bloodline screening program led by the Board of Trustees. Officially, they select elites from students of A-rank or higher for special training. In fact, they have another purpose: to purge suspicious bloodlines among us. These students are all considered to have questionable bloodlines, including your student Chen Motong.” Schneider pointed at Guderian. “And your student Lu Mingfei. Now, my old friends, do you still say this has nothing to do with you?”
“That can't be right. If we're talking about suspicious bloodlines, isn't your student Chu Zihang the most questionable of all? But Chu Zihang isn't in here?” Guderian said.

“Easy to understand,” Manstein said quietly. “He's Chu Zihang's adviser. Even if Chu Zihang is under suspicion, his dossier wouldn't be sent to him. The people he's asked to investigate must have no connection to him.” He already believed Schneider.
“What could be wrong with them? Aren't they all good students, excellent in conduct and academics?” Guderian was bewildered.
“Did you investigate them?” Manstein asked.

“The Board's orders must be carried out. I've already submitted my report. I gathered a little information and wrote something up. I said there was nothing suspicious about their bloodlines, but my conclusion may not be accepted,” Schneider said calmly. “The two most unusual are Lu Mingfei and Chen Motong. They resonate with Draconic, but have no Yanling. Lu Mingfei in particular is the only S-rank student. In other words, his rank is as high as a trustee's, yet he has no Yanling. Anyone could easily grow suspicious of him.”
“What exactly defines a suspicious bloodline?” Manstein asked.

“An excessive proportion of dragon blood. Generally, we believe that if a hybrid's dragon blood exceeds their human blood, they are closer to a dragon than a human. They are no longer one of us. But dragon blood can also be genetically recessive, and those recessive genes may awaken slowly. That can cause a hybrid to become progressively more dragonlike. Once they cross the fifty-percent threshold, they become the enemy,” Schneider said. “The Dragon King Norton is a classic example. He was a pureblood dragon, but before his awakening he believed himself to be a human orphan.”
“Is there any laboratory method now for measuring the genetic proportions?”

“No. We have to rely on analyzing their behavior. So you understand why the Board paid such a high price to steal this archive, and why the recovery operation was assigned such a high priority. Among the students investigated under the Nibelungen Project, Lu Mingfei, Chen Motong, and very likely Chu Zihang all come from China.”
“They're looking into their family histories,” Manstein said quietly.
“Mingfei... can't be a problem. How could he be dangerous? He's a complete coward!” Guderian stammered.
“Haven't you always said your student is inspiration from head to toe?” Manstein pushed him aside and looked at Schneider. “If the Board considers their bloodlines dangerous... what happens?”
“You know how the Board operates as well as I do.” Schneider stopped what he was doing and looked up at Manstein, his iron-gray eyes filled with a bone-deep chill.
Manstein took a deep breath. “The iron-fist rule... purge them!”
“Kill... kill them?” Guderian's voice trembled. “Surely that isn't necessary... Couldn't we buy a little island in the Pacific, build a villa, send them there, and deliver supplies regularly?”
“A lifelong vacation in Hawaii? With treatment that good, I'd want a dangerous bloodline too,” Manstein said with a bitter smile. “But do you think the Board is a group of philanthropists?”
“They wouldn't kill them, but historically they used lobotomy to purge people whose bloodlines were dangerous,” Schneider said.
“What does that mean? I haven't studied brain science.” Guderian stared.

Schneider hesitated. He did not want to bring up this history, but the Secret Party had endured for thousands of years, from the ancient age of blood sacrifice through the dark Middle Ages and the radical industrial era into modern society. Its history could not possibly conform entirely to today's moral standards.

“It's a form of brain surgery invented by António Egas Moniz, a Portuguese physician. Studying ancient Egyptian skulls, he found holes drilled into them and concluded the Egyptians had used brain surgery to treat epilepsy. He developed his theory and believed that removing white matter from the brain's lobes could treat all kinds of mental illness, including such unwelcome states as depression, agitation, anxiety, and paranoia. From 1930 to 1950, tens of thousands of these operations were performed worldwide. The patients really did become more docile and easier to control afterward, but often they sat in one place all day muttering to themselves like fools. He won the Nobel Prize in Medicine for it,” Manstein said. “It's one of the most absurd Nobel Prizes in history, because the doctor completely misunderstood why the Egyptians performed the operation. In the age of the pharaohs, it was used to control hybrids. Removing the lobes also severed the ‘spiritual resonance’ most essential to their dragon blood.”
“The Council of Elders knew what the operation did, so they sent suspected hybrids to psychiatric hospitals...” Schneider said. “They also paid to promote its supposed benefits around the world.”
“Damn...” Guderian murmured.

“By now you should both understand. Some people at the college are suspected of being dangerous, and we are their advisers. If something happens to them, we'll have to bear some of the consequences too, so we need to take action.” Schneider struck a match and set fire to the sheet about Chu Zihang. Amid choking smoke, the film slowly melted in the ashtray.
“Let me borrow a match,” Guderian said.

“Don't bother. There's nothing in the film about Lu Mingfei. The Executive Department investigated his past; it was utterly ordinary. His first eighteen years were so normal they seemed like a failure. You might even suspect he had no bloodline at all and was admitted by mistake.” Schneider shrugged.
“A genius must have something that sets him apart!” Guderian breathed a sigh of relief.
Another match struck. Both men turned to see Manstein expressionlessly lighting a different sheet of film.
“Mr. Chairman of the Disciplinary Committee, that's not your usual style,” Schneider said with a cold smile. “Aren't you the one who values college rules and the Board's orders above all else?”
Manstein did not answer. He watched impassively as the sheet turned to ash in the tray.

Guderian saw the light. “Is it because of her mother? You were secretly in love with her mother back then, weren't you? You're an extraordinary man of loyalty and feeling.” He was delighted, as if he had discovered a new continent, and used a new expression he had recently learned.
“Damn it! Nothing of the sort!” Manstein wanted to smash the ashtray into his face.

Schneider deftly gathered the remaining film, stuffed it back into the aluminum case, and clicked on a new lock he had prepared earlier. He let out a long breath and looked at Guderian and Manstein. “There. It's done. We're accomplices now. We should have a drink together.”
“Wait! You destroyed the paper envelope with the Board's seal. That's too obvious!” Manstein said sharply.
“Simple. The hunters stole these documents, so they must have taken some of the contents.” Schneider was confident. “That's what happened. Entirely reasonable.”

“Some hunters with low-purity bloodlines—why would they meddle in our affairs? If someone hired them in secret, why would they open the documents? They're only people taking commissions to earn a little money.” Manstein frowned. “They had no reason to do that.”
“They're bad people.” Schneider shrugged. “Bad people can do anything. They don't need a reason.”
“Your logic is just like the Executive Department's methods... crude and direct...” Manstein murmured.

A gentle knock sounded at the door. The three exchanged quick glances. Schneider sprang up, grabbed the ashtray, dumped it into the wastebasket, and poured in a can of Coke. Guderian threw a thick dictionary on top, smothering the wisps of smoke. Manstein quickly rearranged his face into the stern integrity expected of the chairman of the Disciplinary Committee. He went to the door and opened it. Outside stood a smiling young man, his long golden hair covering half his remarkably delicate face.
He held out his hand. “Hello, Professor Manstein? I'm Parsi, secretary to the Board of Trustees. I've been sent to collect a case.”

He looked into the central control room. An aluminum case sat on the long table. The imposing, cold-faced Professor Schneider of the Executive Department and Professor Guderian, whistling in apparent boredom, both seemed delighted to see him and waved. “Hi!”
“Damn it! Does he really have to whistle to show he has nothing to hide?” Manstein cursed inwardly.
